977162,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.6.1.2,1932-11-16,b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75,ca.m.2309,Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):,Minister of Trade and Commerce,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR PAPERS,ALBERTA ELEVATORS-OVERAGES,Mr. Speaker, I spoke to this motion on Monday at which time the hon. member was not in the house. I do not know whether or not he has read my remarks, but I might say that I pointed out that it has not been the practice of my or any other department to disclose the operations of any private concern. In the annual report of the Board of Grain Commissioners most complete statements are given of overages and other matters pertaining to the operation of elevators, but it has not been the practice to disclose what each elevator or each company had on hand. My hon. friend wrote the department some time ago and I think the deputy minister replied in much the same manner in which I am now replying. I would suggest to the house that if my hon. friend is agreeable this resolution be dropped for the time being until it is decided whether or not we should disclose the operations of private companies.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Herbert Stevens,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75&Language=E&Section=ALL
977163,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.6.1.3,1932-11-16,bec983fd-5d93-4fb8-b921-3a1d702cbebd,ca.m.3148,Mr. GARLAND (Bow River):,,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR PAPERS,ALBERTA ELEVATORS-OVERAGES,The attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is quite understandable but I would draw his attention to the fact that a few years ago when the Grain Act was under revision a very full list of the names of companies operating and their overages was published and became part of the record. With all due deference to the minister, I fail to see when a company has a certain quantity of goods on hand a.t the end of the year why that information should not be considered as a matter of public concern.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,Edward Joseph Garland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bec983fd-5d93-4fb8-b921-3a1d702cbebd&Language=E&Section=ALL
977164,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.6.1.4,1932-11-16,b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75,ca.m.2309,Mr. STEVENS:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,QUESTIONS,MOTION FOR PAPERS,ALBERTA ELEVATORS-OVERAGES,If my hon. friend will drop the resolution for the time being and talk this matter over with me I am sure we can reach an agreement. There is no desire on my part to withhold any proper information.
Motion dropped.

wish to inquire from the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) who, at present, is acting for the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), whether it is a fact that La Patrie of Montreal has obtained a permit to operate a broadcasting station, under the call CKEP?",,,,

977167,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.7.2,1932-11-16,fc6ff860-be03-4a6f-a606-82cc698f3cdf,ca.m.2832,Hon. MAURICE DUPRE (Acting Minister of Marine) (Translation):,Solicitor General of Canada,QUESTIONS,RADIO COMMISSION,,"Mr. Speaker, in reply I wish to state that, yesterday, I notified my hon. colleague, the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that I would make a

correction, today, to the statement I made yesterday. My statement was that no broadcasting permit had been issued since the Radio Commission had been appointed. I used the word ""appointed."" This may have been the cause of some ambiguity, I therefore wish to dispel such ambiguity, if it exists. I should have said: ""since the commission had been sworn in."" No permit was issued except one-and this is my reply to my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay-of 100 watts to La Patrie. The permit was issued by myself, as interim Minister of Marine, previously, however, to the commission being sworn in, the latter had no say in the matter.

FERNAND RINFRET (St. James) (Translation):,,QUESTIONS,SOCKEYE SALMON TREATY,,Mr. Speaker, I also wish to put a question to the Acting Minister of Marine (Mr. Dupre). As he is aware, the navigation season will soon close; generally, the employees whose services have been required during that season are placed at the disposal of the board of harbour commissioners. I wish to inquire whether it would be possible, this year, to request these various boards, especially those connected with inland harbours, such as Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal, to employ, as much as possible, on winter work, the men who were at their service during the summer season.

GORDON (Minister of Labour) :,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,QUESTIONS,SOCKEYE SALMON TREATY,,Since, I believe, November, 1930, after a very thorough investigation of the condition in which soldier settlers in common with many others found themselves, I caused the various superintendents throughout Canada to be circularized by the then board and afterwards by the director, the instructions in substance being that every possible leniency be extended to soldier settlers; that where it appeared that a soldier settler, not through malingering, being able to pay just refused to pay, but through misadventure was unable to make his payments falling due on account of his loan, then in no case should departmental action be taken that would prompt or cause such a settler to leave his homestead. That policy has been consistently followed, is being followed today and will continue to be followed until prices revive and the settlers are in better condition.

Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): I have a question to address to the Minister of Labour who is always very good in giving any information he can. Since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), has given to the house and the country approximately the number of unemployed according to the census of 1931 and since, by additions thereto, at the present moment we have over 700,000 unemployed in Canada, may I ask the minister if he can give to parliament approximately the total number directly and indirectly on dominion relief at the present moment?",,,,

977208,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.11.2,1932-11-16,e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072,ca.m.5276,Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) :,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,QUESTIONS,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,,"I do not know that I can be so

specific as to answer the question as ""at the present moment."" It would be rather difficult for me to do so. Again, it is rather difficult to define ""unemployed."" That has given rise to difficulties that confront anyone who tries to make an estimate. But I shall say that the total number, men, women and children, on relief, I think for the last month, is something over 800,000. I may say that that includes 144,000 who, according to governmental figures covering a period of ten years from 1919 to 1929, have been on the average unemployed. It also includes some 140,000, sometimes called transients, and as nearly as the Department of Labour can estimate, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 50 per cent of those-and probably it is more than that-are very new arrivals in Canada.

977211,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.12.2,1932-11-16,e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072,ca.m.5276,Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) :,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,QUESTIONS,SOLDIER SETTLEMENT-MR. F. N. MURPHY,,Yesterday the hon. member for North
Soldier Settlement
Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), asked me a question in connection with soldier settlers. This question, which is to be found on page 1147 of Hansard, is as follows:

I have a question to direct to the Minister of Labour. I have in my possession correspondence in connection with a returned soldier by the name of F. N. Murphy, of northern Saskatchewan, who joined the first battalion early in the war and was demobilized in 1919. When he returned he was placed on land purchased by his father. The father never lived on the land, the soldier himself having lived there from the time it was purchased. Since this man has not had any revaluation of that land, no discount, while others who apparently were never in the front line trenches have had a revaluation, will the minister investigate the matter and see that justice is meted out to this returned man, who is trying to make a living on that land in northern Saskatchewan.

I made answer from memory to that question yesterday, but since then I have had an opportunity to inquire into the details of the matter and my answer of yesterday is borne out by the fact. Shortly put, Eugene Murphy, father of P. N. Murphy, the man to whom reference was made, entered into an agreement as a civilian with the then soldier settlement board on September 13, 1921, to purchase the west half of 28-47-6- west of the third meridian. Neither in the application to purchase nor in the agreement for sale nor in any subsequent correspondence between the department and Eugene Murphy was there any intent disclosed that he was merely buying this land for his son.

With respect to revaluation of soldier settlers' lands, I would refer the hon. member to section 68 of the Soldier Settlement Act. At the time the revaluation amendment was passed in 1927, F. N. Murphy was not a settler who had agreed to purchase any land from the board and consequently, although a returned soldier, was not entitled to benefit under that legislation. The father, Eugene Murphy, who had agreed to purchase the property from the board, being a civilian, was not entitled to benefit under the revaluation measure. The legislation with respect to the thirty per cent reduction became effective on May 30, 1930. On the decease of Eugene Murphy, the executor assigned the title and interest of the late Eugene Murphy in the agreement to which I have made reference to F. N. Murphy. F. N. Murphy was at no time qualified or established in accordance with the provisions of the act and regulations, which latter are statutory and define the powers of the department with respect to the establishment of settlers and the manner in which settlers may be qualified with a view to

such establishment. It may be observed further that F. N. Murphy is a settler who holds, not an agreement for sale with the department, but an assignment and extension of his late father's agreement and is not eligible under the provisions of the amendment above referred to to participate in the benefits thereunder.

The position is very plain. I was not a member of the House of Commons when the legislation was passed in 1927. I have no complaint to make as to the effect of that legislation, but I am sure that the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) in making the observations he did yesterday was misinformed as to what the facts were. I believe that he was a member of this chamber when that legislation was passed and must have known that the soldier to whom he referred could not by any stretch of the imagination become entitled to a revaluation under the legislation.

it to him. I sat quietly last night while the hon. gentleman spoke about the dumping duty on cigarettes and how much more must be paid, and said that Great Britain could not break through the barricade because of that dumping duty. There is no dumping duty on cigarettes; there is no dumping duty on anything that pays an excise tax, and I believe my hon. friend, with his experience, must know something about that. Now the hon. gentleman has instanced this last case, and he wants to know how business can be expected with Great Britain exporting under a 31 per cent duty as against a 25 per cent duty to the United States.
A moment ago an hon. gentleman opposite gave the case of a Canadian importer taking $100 with -which he desired to buy goods. As every hon. member knows who has considered the question

as I am sure the hon. member for Weyburn has considered it-in the country with the currency depreciated to the greatest extent you can buy the greatest amount of goods for your money. Surely that is plain. So what happens to the importer with his S100? He goes to Great Britain and pays less there and contributes more to the revenue. If he goes to France or to the Netherlands with his $100 he pays more to the man who sells him the goods and contributes less to the revenue. The astute English business men who were over here asked for the chance to do business with us, and with the pound depreciated this will work to their advantage. Surely my hon. friend will not object if the revenue of this country is increased. That is the situation. One hundred dollars is not a constant sum all through the game. You can get more goods for less money in Great Britain and contribute more to the revenue, while in France you get less goods and pay the country a smaller sum. It is very simple.

977420,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.177,1932-11-16,b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75,ca.m.2309,Mr. STEVENS:,Minister of Trade and Commerce,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,The answer to my hon. friend is under his nose. This article is free, and we cannot make it any more free. My hon. friend also says that Great Britain has undertaken that if certain things happen the preference will be taken off. We are taking off the duty before we start, because glass is to come in free. While we differ from the hon. member very markedly in the theories he propounds in regard to tariffs and other matters, at least we have always given him credit for being sincere and fair. But is he fair in his criticism of the Prime Minister and the government in connection with the glass episode of two years ago? What happened? Down to a certain point the hon. member set out the facts correctly, but at that point his prejudice prevented him from giving just a little bit of credit to the government for something they did. What happened? The moment it was clear-and it did not take long to make it clear-I will go farther and say the moment there was evidence the company was about to break faith, or did not intend to keep faith, the Prime Minister, who was in London at the time, was cabled by his colleagues in Canada. Immediately a cable was sent back which said, ""Take that duty off."" That was a very salutary action, because it showed the industries of Canada-and there are many industrialists who are prepared to
take advantage of conditions-that as far as this government is concerned they had broken faith with an undertaking, and that the government would not tolerate such action.

Whatever else my hon. friend may charge us with, whatever else he may say concerning our policies, no matter what his condemnations of our actions may be, I suggest that at least he should have the courtesy to extend credit to the Prime Minister and government when they took action promptly, expeditiously and definitely. In connection with these items I fail to understand the attitude of the hon. member. What have we done in this instance? So far as Great Britain is concerned we have taken off the duty in the glass schedule. My colleague the Minister of Finance has stated clearly,-and I am prepared to corroborate everything he has said,- that the glass industry of Great Britain is by no means tied up in a cartel. There is competition, keen competition, and there is no doubt in the minds of the British government, the British delegation or the British glass industry that this is one of the most valuable things we can give Great Britain under the treaty.

Here is an instance where we meet the views of the leader of the opposition. He has complained that we have not eliminated the duty in connection with many items, and has asked why we did not lower the rates. In this instance we have wiped them out. Could we do more? The hon. member for Weyburn has said that this is a farce and that it is of no value. But I ask him this question: Could we do any more than we have done? I think if he will reflect for a moment concerning the action of the government in connection with a Canadian industry which had received protection two years ago, and had failed to carry out its obligations, he will decide that the government acted in a most expeditious manner, and that the removal of the protection offered at that time was in the interests of Canada. He must further agree that in this instance, where we have placed glass on the free list, we have done all he could have asked us to do, no matter what his theories or ideas may be.

318 I should like to point out that while the Minister of Trade and Commerce has complained that hon. members on this side of the house have not been quite fair, in giving reasons why the government have abolished the duty on plain glass he himself was not fair. What are the facts? I believe it was on September 17, 1930, that the item was first dealt with. At that time the tariff on imports of plain glass was changed from per cent ad valorem to a specific duty of 4J cents per pound.

Immediately, on September 23, two or three days after the change had been made, importers of glass in Canada sent out circular letters in which they pointed out that on account of this increase in duty a 120 pound box of plain glass which had formerly cost $5.63 would have to be sold wholesale for a little over $11. I remember well that when the change was made I pointed out that it could not be satisfactory. I asked the minister if it would not be possible to leave the item, and to make a provision in it to the effect that when a Canadian firm could supply the demand, the specific duty should apply. The reply from the Prime Minister was that the item could not be so treated. He said they had received an absolute guarantee from a firm in East Hamilton that the increase in duty would not involve an increased price to. the consumers. What are the facts? The letter from the' firm in east Hamilton did not lay down any such proposition. The letter laid down this proposition: As the cost of production is lowered by the increased production we will give the benefit of the lower cost to the consumer.

977541,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.298,1932-11-16,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,The Minister

of National Revenue says that this ought to help trade with Great Britain. May I say that I believe every hon. member on this side of the house is desirous of trading with Great Britain to as large an extent as possible so long as we can get for our money goods of equal value in quantity and quality. But on what grounds can the Minister of National Revenue justify any government taking away from the people the right to purchase where they please with what is the fruit of their labour, whether it be manual or intellectual labour? Surely one thing a man possesses with which he has a right to do as he pleases is the fruit of his own effort, whether put forth by hand or brain. What right has any government to say that he shall not be free to get the real value, not the nominal value merely of his labour, wherever he pleases? A man is paid wages for his labour or receives a salary for intellectual and other services; that is the nominal reward, the real reward is what that money will buy. When the Minister of National Revenue says that we must buy from Britain even if we have to pay a higher price for the commodities or accept commodities of a poorer quality, it seems to me that he is asserting on behalf of the government a power which no government has the right to exercise over the people, and which cannot be defended. I should like to hear the minister's defence of taking away from the people in this manner a part of their income; for that is what he is doing. It is an arbitrary method of taking from wage and salary earners a portion of their incomes as expressed in the real commodities which they can buy with the fruits of their labour.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL

There is nothing new about that. I did not say to the right hon. gentleman that we "" must "" buy from Britain, but the object of this tariff, of the items wdiich have been considered and are afterwards to be considered, was, without wrecking any established interests, to influence trade to travel between the different countries of the empire. I think that that object has boon well accomplished in what has been done. All these tariff items were not fixed by us. There were two parties to the agreement, and the other party had to be considered. They knew what they wanted, and some of the items here represent what they wanted. The charge is made in England that we got the advantage, and the charge has been made in Canada, and in this house, that they got the advantage. But it is idle to say that wTe are interfering with the rights of the workingman or with the privileges of the people of Canada because under this item the duty is being raised fifty cents a ton in the one case and seventy-five cents in the other. To make that contention seems almost foolish, if I may use the word. This is the point that should be considered. These items are not ours unless we agreed to them. It may be that we should not have agreed to some of them if they had not been asked for, but we acceded to them because we felt that we also were getting advantages in the agreement. The agreement, I submit, is altogether consonant with the rights of every citizen of Canada, but the trouble with my right hon. friend and those whom he leads is that they want to buy from foreign countries whenever they possibly can instead of trading, as I submit should be done, in the interests of the empire.

But referring first of all to the comparison he made between these tariffs and the tariffs under the previous administration, may I point out that under the previous Liberal administration the tariff in Canada was lowered time and time again to afford more in the way of freedom of opportunity to purchase commodities wherever the individuals in this country might wish to purchase them, and to provide more in the way of freedom of trade. Under the present government the tariff has been in-
United Kingdom

creased time and time again until it has now reached prohibitive heights. It has made trade altogether impossible, and according to the Prime Minister apparently that has been done deliberately with a view of preventing trade with other countries.

The Minister of National Revenue knows he is quite wrong when he says that we on this side of the house prefer to trade with foreign countries rather than with Britain. Let me tell him that the opposite is the case. We prefer to trade with Britain, other things being equal, but we do not propose to be told that we must trade with Britain no matter how adverse an influence that trade may have on our incomes. When you reach a point in the imposition of tariffs that you no longer receive revenue from them, when the tariff becomes prohibitive to that extent, its effect is simply to prevent trading, and it becomes an income tax in another form. It means that the individual-and the smaller his income the more he will feel the tax-is no longer able to purchase with his income the same number of commodities or get the same satisfaction of his wants which he otherwise would be able to get. It simply becomes a means of increasing the cost of living all around.

column1: 977574,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.331,1932-11-16,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,"This is a

terrible one. The general tariff on plates of iron or steel has been increased from $7 to $8 under (a); the intermediate tariff has been increased from S6 to $8, so that both intermediate and general are placed on the same level. Then under (b) there is an increase in the general tariff from $5 to $6 and in the intermediate from $3 to $6-it is doubled- and British preference is left the same in each case. Those two items alone, will serve materially to increase the cost of construction and other items that enter into general production costs and costs of living in this country.

three preceding items we passed showed very substantial reductions in the British preference. Naturally they passed by without comment. I do not complain of that. In the case of the increases to which my right hon. friend has just now referred, in most instances they are relatively less than they were under the Dunning budget. There the increase in one particular item that I have in. mind was from $2.50 general to $4.50, almost double, whereas in this case the increase is from $6 to $8 and $7 to $8. So the relative increase is very much less than on the item to which I have referred.

977600,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.357,1932-11-16,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,This helps to

illustrate the really protective intent of this particular change. The old rate was 7i per cent, 12J per cent and 12 V per cent, while the new rates are 7i per cent, 20 per cent and 20 per cent. The minister just told us that the importations last year amounted to $2,226,000, of which $340,000 came from Great Britain. The rate remains the same on imports under the British preference, but is increased from 124 per cent to 20 per cent under the general and intermediate tariffs. As the general and intermediate rates carry the bulk of the imports, and the tariff is unchanged under the British preference, the item constitutes an increase under the general and intermediate tariffs of 60 per cent. The added cost to the Canadian consumers, if the imports remained the same, would be $140,000, and to this must be added whatever extra charges may be made by the Canadian manufacturers who will now enjoy an increase of 60 per cent in their protection. This is a drastic increase made under the pretence of aiding Great Britain.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL

In dealing with any one of a dozen countries with depreciated currencies it is obligatory under the law that those currencies shall be considered as of a certain value. When an article enters the country the customs officer must look up the quotations on the milreis, the lira, the franc, the yen, the tael, the dollar, the pound or other currency, depending upon where the article originates. During the war, and in recent years, when exchange rates were fluctuating repeatedly, it has been and is the custom to stabilize such rates for a week or two; an artificial exchange rate is declared, otherwise it would be hopeless to ask the customs officials all over Canada to be posted upon the day to day or hour to hour rates. Sometimes these set rates may be good for a year; it depends entirely upon the fluctuations in exchange as between this and other countries. The customs officer turns to his bulletin and gets the rate of exchange, and if the article in question has come from a country with a depreciated currency, under the regulations and the statute he must impose a penalty, if my hon. friend chooses to call it such, or an exchange adjustment duty, as I prefer to call it, which brings the invoice price up to that figure. I will not say that these fluctuations occur daily in connection with all countries, but they occur often enough to prove to be a confusing factor. It would be quite fruitless for us to take an item, strike an exchange rate which we think is right, and start to figure on that basis. As an example, let us take the differential in exchange between here and the United States. If we have a 30 per cent duty against a certain article coming from the United States, when that article enters Canada the Canadian purchaser must find dollars to pay for it in addition to paying the 30 per cent duty, and for those dollars he pays 13 per cent in exchange. He pays not a 13 per cent penalty but a 13 per cent premium upon American dollars 'with which to pay his indebtedness. My hon. friend will see that that is a factor which must be always borne in mind. In making his calculation my hon. friend adds or subtracts, as the case may be; he takes that differential in exchange and calls it a customs duty. It is not a customs duty at all; it may have a similar effect, but it is an exchange factor due to the necessity of buying other currencies with Canadian funds. Perhaps my bon. friend will accept the suggestion of the Minister of Finance, that we fake, say steel or iron or something which has a common factor where there is a world price, shall I say, in Pittsburgh or London, and figure out
United Kingdom

a comparison on certain commodities and give it to my hon. friend tomorrow. We do not wish to be discourteous; we do not wish to say to my hon. friend each time: We do not agree with your figuring; we think you are wrong. I am quite certain the gentleman who has helped my hon. friend to do his figuring-my hon. friend will admit he has a good adviser in this-could undoubtedly figure it out quite well; but I think in some of the figures he gave he was calculating on the basis of a rate of exchange that must have been applicable a month or two ago. The normal value of the pound is $4.86}. The government has said that it should be $4.40. The actual value fluctuates from day to day, so to avoid the difficulty my hon. friend mentions of having to take account of the fluctuations from day to day, every two weeks the department sets an average value for those two weeks. The other day, November 10, it issued this bulletin: ""The average value of the pound sterling declared by the department for special duty purposes is $3.71, effective for entries during the period November 16 to 30, 1932."" The actual value of the pound yesterday was $3.73 Canadian funds. The government had declared the average value for the present two weeks to be $3.71. They have also declared that the pound should be $4.40. I have been calling it an exchange dumping duty, but my hon. friend prefers to call it an exchange adjustment duty. I do not care what he calls it; it is a duty anyway; but that duty, whatever it is, shall be the difference between $4.40 and the rate they have fixed of $3.71, or sixty-nine cents. So that particular duty will be sixty-nine cents on an investment of Canadian money of $3.73. It is only a simple matter in artih-metic to figure out that that amounts to 18} per cent. That is how I have arrived at this exchange adjustment duty, if my hon. friend prefers to call it that.

What I have been asking all along is that the minister take the ad valorem or specific rate, or both, as the case may be, based not on the invoice value of the goods in Canadian currency, but on what is declared to be the value for duty; figure that out; add to it this 18} per cent and whatever the excise tax amounts to, and give us the total. In addition I believe there is ten per cent off the regular duty for direct shipment. That can be figured out. The arrangement the government has made for fixing every two weeks the average value of the pound in Canadian currency will avoid the difficulty of coming to an actual estimate. I do not see why we cannot have that total rate submitted to the committee in a few minutes. When we are passing these items, we have a right to know what the actual rate is going to be. The Economist has prepared a special supplement dealing with the Ottawa agreements. It is a careful statement of the effect of the tariff changes, and I should like to read to my hon. friend one of the paragraphs which deals with this matter. The statement is:

The (Canadian) tariff is, however, payable on the value of the article translated into dollars at the rate of $4.86 to the pound, and not at the actual rate of about $3.70 to the pound. In many eases this provision alone neutralizes the British preference in comparison with countries which are on the gold standard.

In addition to the ordinary tariffs, imports into Canada are chargeable with three other taxes. The first of these is the sales tax, now at the rate of 6 per cent, -which is not essentially protective, since it is also payable on home products.
excise tax, amounting to 3 per cent, which, despite its name, is payable only on imports.
United Kingdom

These two taxes, making a charge of 9 per cent, are levied upon the value of the imports plus the tariff which has been paid. Thus, if $100 of imports are subject to a tariff of 30 per cent, these taxes will amount to 9 per cent of $130. or $11.70.

The third of the special taxes is the dumping duty. Until recently, this duty had scarcely any effect upon United Kingdom trade, because it was most unusual for traders in this country to sell their goods in Canada at a price below that charged here. But, owing to the fact that the Canadian government fix arbitrary and different values for the exchange of pounds into dollars when calculating prices in the United Kingdom and in Canada, this duty has become a heavy charge upon British imports into Canada. Under the ordinary regulations concerning this duty if an imported article is offered for sale in Canada at a price less than its ""fair market value"" in the country of origin, a duty equal to the difference between these prices' is payable. At the present time (i.e., the period October 16 to 31, 1932) the value of the pound is declared fixed at $3.82 for the purpose of calculating the selling price of British goods in Canada; but for the purpose of determining ""fair market value"" in the United Kingdom the pound is at present fixed at $4.40. Hence, at the rates now in operation, if the price of an article in pounds is identical here and in Canada, it is still necessary to pay a dumping duty amounting to 58 cents for everv pound of the value.

This dutv in particular has met with much opposition from Canadian importers of British goods, and even before Ottawa expectations had arisen that it would be reduced. These expecta-, tions themselves at the present time are an additional barrier to British trade, because they lead importers to delay buying stocks from the United Kingdom pending a reduction with the consequence that, when orders have to be executed at short notice, they frequently go to the United States.
I think that that is an exact statement of the situation with which it purports to deal. If in any particular it is wrong, will some member of the ministry please so inform the committee?

977648,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.405,1932-11-16,0f69931c-5158-425e-825a-70935470915d,ca.m.528,Mr. YOUNG:,,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,No, it is not carried. The minister has given reasons why the government does not care to make the computations for which I have asked. They would not like to risk the reputation of any of the experts in government departments. They suggest hasty computations are unfair, and perhaps we cannot blame them. But I have no such reputation at stake, and I am willing to make a computation. If I am wrong, perhaps the ministers opposite will put me right. I have made a computation of what the actual applied rate will go on one British pound sterling worth of goods described in item 354a as kitchen or household hollowware of aluminum. It figures out like this: The quoted rate here from Great Britain is 20 per cent. That will be applied on $4.86f although the goods only cost $3.73 Canadian. This 20 per cent on $4.86 is equal to 26 per cent on $3.73; that would be the ad valorem rate. There is a ten per cent reduction if the goods are shipped direct to Canada, which would leave it 23-4 per cent. Then the special excise tax of 3 per cent, which is in reality a duty, will be based on $1-234 or 3-7 per cent. The exchange adjustment duty -my hon. friend preferred to call it by that name rather than exchange dumping duty- will be 18-5 per cent, making 45-6 per cent. In addition to that we have a portion of the 6 per cent sales tax. So my estimate is that the actual charges applied against a British shipment of these goods would be 47 per cent or more. If I am wrong, let the experts of the department say so. But I make this offer to the minister; I am willing to drop this whole matter until all these items are through the committee if the minister will promise that when we get into ways and means he will furnish us with another column to this schedule showing the actual applied rate, all things included, on all goods coming from within the British Empire.

I suppose the last consumer would be according to my hon. friend's reasoning, the company that does the construction work on the bridge. I can understand the government permitting the iron and steel industry to divide up the British Empire amongst themselves and arrange what will be one man's finished product will be another's raw material, but to arrive at what will be paid by the consumer and taxpayer, in the last analysis we have to go as far as the users of the commodities. 977832,ca.proc.d.1932-11-16.1.17.589,1932-11-16,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OP BILL NO. 8,,The Minister of Finance keeps talking about the British representatives being satisfied. I should think they ought to be, and I should think the Canadian manufacturers ought to be satisfied, because together they have been given a monopoly of the British empire on iron and steel-that is what it means. They could not ask for much more. But why does the minister not speak in terms of the Canadian consumers, the people of Canada who have to buy these materials and who use the articles into which in part they enter? No item could better illustrate what I have been pointing out. that under the pretext of doing something for British trade the present administration is really seeking to raise tariffs to create monopolies for special interests in the British Empire, and to exclude the foreigner. Let me illustrate; The present British preference on this item, $4.25 per ton, has been lowered to $4. Twenty-five cents per ton is the extent of the reduction in favour of Great Britain. Look at what has taken place in the matter of tariff increase. The general tariff has been increased from $7 to $8 per ton and the intermediate from $6 to $8 per ton, an increase of $1 and $2 respectively, and there is a reduction of only 25 cents in the British preferential rate. As was pointed out, only 18 tons came into Canada from Great Britain in an entire year; all the rest were entered under the intermediate or general tariff. Nothing could make it clearer that the whole purpose is to help privileged interests in the monopoly which has been given them by the government.

In other words the whole business of the empire was divided among the manufacturers in the empire. The rate on this particular class of steel was $4.25 per ton under the previous budget, and the spread between the British preferential rate and the intermediate rate was $1.75. So the only preference the British manufacturer was given in this market was $1.75. He could not raise his price more than 81.75 without coming into competition with Belgium and the United States. The minister must see that, this agreement being for five years, and it being stated that the differential must be maintained, the British manufacturer who has been given the trade in this specific item, apparently by common consent, can if he so chooses, and if the minister does not wish to take advantage of his power under section 17 of the Customs Tariff, ride up to $1.50 or $2 a ton more than normal price, because the market is his. about the possibility of the British manufacturer taking advantage of the changes in the schedule to increase the price to Canadian consumers, would the minister kindly note this point: let us take item 383:
(a) Coated with tin, of a class or kind not made in Canada, n.o.p.

This commodity is not made in Canada; it has to come from Britain. Under the British preference it is free at the present time and it was free formerly, but whereas the intermediate and general rates were formerly only five per cent, they have now been raised to 15 per cent. What is to prevent the British manufacturer from immediately increasing his prices to the extent of the difference between the five per cent and the 15 per cent or increasing his price to the 15 per cent limit? There is nothing whatever to prevent him from doing that. The point, however, which I want to bring out at the moment, and which I do not think has been brought out as yet, makes the situation even worse. It is this: Under this agreement we have tied ourselves to abide for five years by the increased price which may be levied. What applies to this item applies to every case where there is a margin of preference. In other words, once the British manufacturer has seen his chance of increasing his price and has shoved it up to the limit of his opportunity, not only is there no redress by way of taking from him any benefit he may derive from any duty, because the item is free under the British preference; he actually can laugh at the Canadian government and people and say: Your government has agreed that you will be bound for five years by the margin of preference which has been fixed and you cannot alter that margin. And that margin in this case would give him 15 per cent, which is the rate under general and intermediate tariffs.

In the old days, as my hon. friend well knows, before a revision of the tariff was attempted there was something in the nature of a tariff commission appointed. It used to be composed of members of the administration, who went from one end of the country to the other, and if tariff changes were sought the parties desiring them were allowed to appear and make out their case. Other parties were also heard, the farmers were given opportunity to state their views, consumers generally were allowed to appear and state their views, with the result that when the government came to the House of Commons with its proposed tariff changes it was able to give the reasons why the tariffs were being fixed at particular rates. Later, when that practice was discontinued, there was established a tariff advisory board, and before that board parties likely to be affected by any change in the tariff were given opportunity to be heard; so that when the Minister of Finance was presenting his budget with its tariff changes he was in a position to say, not merely that one party in interest had been heard, but that all parties had been heard and given a chance to state how they would be affected by the changes.

Now my hon. friend tells us: This was agreed to at the conference. Let us follow that. The conference was a secret conclave, no one except the members of the administration who were present knows anything about what took place, or is supposed to know. In other words the public, the ones who are affected by what has taken place, have no knowledge whatever of the reasons which actuated the administration, and the administration is now unable to give reasons, beyond ""this is what was agreed to."" And, as the minister told us a few minutes ago, agreed to as a result of discussions between the manufacturing interests in the old country and the manufacturing industries in Canada, the special interests which are being given added favours. How the government can expect the people of the country to have any confidence in a tariff fashioned in that way I fail to see.

[Mr. Rhodes.!

vision of the tariff, that is the bringing down of a budget and dealing with tariff items therein, I am in entire accord. But my right hon. friend must realize that it is a far different matter when you are dealing with an agreement, as we are at the present time. Of necessity conferences have to be in secret. It would be unthinkable-I do not know that in all history it has ever been otherwise- that agreements should be entered into between one nation and another in any other manner. My right hon. friend must also bear in mind that it very frequently happens, I might almost say invariably, that in the course of negotiations a country will grant in respect to individual commodities more concessions than it would at first be disposed to agree to, and the other might do the same thing. In the final analysis, in order to bring about a meeting of minds, there is compromise. Therefore with respect to individual items such as the one in question, it is impossible for me to give my right hon. friend any other reply than I have given. I submit that on this point there is a distinct difference between tariff items which arise by reason of an agreement between nations, and tariff items which are dealt with in the ordinary way in respect of a budget. In the latter case the question which my right hon. friend asked would be susceptible of answer, because it would be the direct result of the government's action with respect to its particular policy. In the case of an agreement it might be-I do not say it is-that in respect to these items we might very well have desired to carry them at the same relative levels a3 they heretofore held, but as a result of the conference discussions this is what emerged as something upon which ultimately we all could agree.
